public_rationale: A systematic review published before the post found recurring customer recognition of flawed code and difficulties making it production-ready. Customers could recognize those limits while still valuing speed and continuing to use the tools. This supports the ordinary reading of emerging recognition. It does not establish universal agreement or a measured change across the entire customer population.
limitations: The study analyzes self-selected public accounts and explicitly limits generalization.
It was a preprint when published.
A strict interpretation of finally as a measured change over time would remain unresolved.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Vibe coding customers are now realizing that the tools are unreliable and unsuited to complex real-world apps.

statement.excerpt: Customers are finally figuring that out.

from_speaker: not for complex apps in the real world
our_interpretation: The ordinary reading is that customers were recognizing reliability, production-readiness and maintenance limitations by the post date.
Recognition does not require abandoning the tools, reducing use or rejecting their benefits.
Customers means users of these tools; the claim supplies neither a paying-customer restriction nor a majority threshold.
I use 2025 through the post date as the current customer-experience period. Finally indicates emerging recognition, without specifying a measurable rate of change.
criteria.support_condition: Systematically collected customer accounts or surveys show recurring recognition that rapid initial results do not make these tools dependable for complex applications without substantial debugging, verification or maintenance work.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable direct evidence shows that recognition of these limitations was exceptional and customers generally considered the tools dependable for complex applications without substantial corrective work. Growth or continued use alone cannot contradict the claim.

evidence.locator: Section 5.1, The Speed–Quality Trade-off Paradox; supporting analysis in Section 4.3
evidence.publisher: arXiv; Ahmed Fawzy, Amjed Tahir and Kelly Blincoe
evidence.explanation: The researchers analyzed 101 practitioner sources containing 518 firsthand behavioral accounts. Their quality-perception analysis documents recognition of flawed outputs, production-readiness difficulties and maintenance costs, while also documenting continued enthusiasm and use.
